claim: Fungi employ LysM effectors to prevent recognition of cell wall-derived chitin by host immune receptors.
source: Fungi employ LysM effectors to prevent recognition of cell wall-derived chitin by host immune receptors, although the mechanism to compete for chitin binding remained unclear.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established knowledge about fungal LysM effectors.

claim: The mechanism for LysM effectors to compete for chitin binding was previously unclear.
source: Fungi employ LysM effectors to prevent recognition of cell wall-derived chitin by host immune receptors, although the mechanism to compete for chitin binding remained unclear.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a knowledge gap.

claim: Ecp6 has three LysM domains.
source: The three LysMs of Ecp6 (LysM1–LysM3) share the typical βααβ-fold, with LysM1 being separated by a long and flexible linker from a compact and rigid body formed by LysM2 and LysM3 (Figure 1A).
evidence: The text explicitly describes the three LysM domains and their structural arrangement.

claim: Ecp6 binds chitin through intrachain LysM dimerization involving LysM1 and LysM3.
source: Structural analysis of the LysM effector Ecp6 of the fungal tomato pathogen Cladosporium fulvum reveals a novel mechanism for chitin binding, mediated by intrachain LysM dimerization, leading to a chitin-binding groove that is deeply buried in the effector protein.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this as a finding from structural analysis.

claim: The composite LysM1-LysM3 binding site of Ecp6 involves two of the three LysMs.
source: This composite binding site involves two of the three LysMs of Ecp6 and mediates chitin binding with ultra-high (pM) affinity.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this structural finding.

claim: The LysM1-LysM3 composite binding site of Ecp6 binds chitin with picomolar (pM) affinity.
source: This composite binding site involves two of the three LysMs of Ecp6 and mediates chitin binding with ultra-high (pM) affinity.
evidence: The abstract states this as a finding from binding studies.

claim: The singular LysM2 domain of Ecp6 binds chitin with low micromolar affinity.
source: Intriguingly, the remaining singular LysM domain of Ecp6 binds chitin with low micromolar affinity but can nevertheless still perturb chitin-triggered immunity.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this binding affinity measurement.

claim: LysM2 of Ecp6 can perturb chitin-triggered immunity despite its lower binding affinity.
source: Intriguingly, the remaining singular LysM domain of Ecp6 binds chitin with low micromolar affinity but can nevertheless still perturb chitin-triggered immunity.
evidence: The abstract states this as an experimental finding.

claim: LysM2 may perturb chitin-triggered immunity through interference with the host immune receptor complex rather than chitin sequestration.
source: Conceivably, the perturbation by this LysM domain is not established through chitin sequestration but possibly through interference with the host immune receptor complex.
evidence: The abstract presents this as a speculative interpretation of the data.

claim: Many fungal species are causative agents of disease in plants.
source: Although most species are saprophytic, many are causative agents of disease and include plant pathogens that cause considerable yield losses in agricultural crops worldwide (Skamnioti and Gurr, 2009; Oliver, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Fungal plant pathogens cause considerable yield losses in agricultural crops worldwide.
source: Although most species are saprophytic, many are causative agents of disease and include plant pathogens that cause considerable yield losses in agricultural crops worldwide (Skamnioti and Gurr, 2009; Oliver, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Hosts employ cell surface receptors to detect conserved pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs) to activate immunity.
source: To sense the presence of potential pathogens, hosts employ cell surface receptors that detect conserved pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs) to activate immunity (Medzhitov and Janeway, 1997; Boller and Felix, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Chitin is an N-acetyl-D-glucosamine (GlcNAc) homopolymer.
source: Chitin, an N-acetyl-D-glucosamine (GlcNAc) homopolymer, is the primary structural component of fungal cell walls and is recognized as a PAMP by plant cell surface receptors that contain extracellular lysin motifs (LysMs) (Felix et al., 1993; Shibuya et al., 1993; Shibuya et al., 1996; Kombrink et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge.

claim: Chitin is the primary structural component of fungal cell walls.
source: Chitin, an N-acetyl-D-glucosamine (GlcNAc) homopolymer, is the primary structural component of fungal cell walls and is recognized as a PAMP by plant cell surface receptors that contain extracellular lysin motifs (LysMs) (Felix et al., 1993; Shibuya et al., 1993; Shibuya et al., 1996; Kombrink et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Chitin is recognized as a PAMP by plant cell surface receptors containing extracellular LysM motifs.
source: Chitin, an N-acetyl-D-glucosamine (GlcNAc) homopolymer, is the primary structural component of fungal cell walls and is recognized as a PAMP by plant cell surface receptors that contain extracellular lysin motifs (LysMs) (Felix et al., 1993; Shibuya et al., 1993; Shibuya et al., 1996; Kombrink et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: CEBiP is the first chitin receptor cloned from rice.
source: The first chitin receptor has been cloned from rice (Oryza sativa) as the chitin oligosaccharide elicitor-binding protein (CEBiP; Kaku et al., 2006) that forms a receptor complex in a ligand-dependent manner that furthermore includes the chitin elicitor receptor kinase-1 (OsCERK1; Shimizu et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kaku et al., 2006.

claim: CEBiP forms a receptor complex with OsCERK1 in a ligand-dependent manner.
source: The first chitin receptor has been cloned from rice (Oryza sativa) as the chitin oligosaccharide elicitor-binding protein (CEBiP; Kaku et al., 2006) that forms a receptor complex in a ligand-dependent manner that furthermore includes the chitin elicitor receptor kinase-1 (OsCERK1; Shimizu et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Arabidopsis thaliana CERK1 binds chitin and is required for chitin-triggered immunity.
source: Similarly, Arabidopsis thaliana CERK1 binds chitin and is required for chitin-triggered immunity (Miya et al., 2007; Wan et al., 2008; Iizasa et al., 2010; Petutschnig et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: No homologs of rice CEBiP could be implicated in chitin-triggered immunity against fungal infection in Arabidopsis.
source: However, no homologs of rice CEBiP could be implicated in chitin-triggered immunity against fungal infection in Arabidopsis (Shinya et al., 2012; Wan et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The crystal structure of the AtCERK1 ectodomain reveals chitin binding to one of the three AtCERK1 LysMs only.
source: Recently, a crystal structure of the AtCERK1 ectodomain was determined, revealing chitin binding to one of the three AtCERK1 LysMs only (Protein Data Bank code 4EBZ; Liu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Liu et al., 2012 and reference to a PDB structure.

claim: LysM2 of AtCERK1 binds three GlcNAc residues of a longer chitin oligomer in a shallow groove on the surface of the protein.
source: LysM2 of AtCERK1 binds three GlcNAc residues of a longer chitin oligomer in a shallow groove on the surface of the protein, with both ends of the oligomer as well as one half side of each of the three bound GlcNAc residues protruding into the solvent (Liu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Liu et al., 2012.

claim: Sufficiently long chitin oligomers act as bivalent ligands, leading to ligand-induced AtCERK1 dimerization required for immune signaling.
source: Biochemical experiments suggest that sufficiently long chitin oligomers act as bivalent ligands, leading to ligand-induced AtCERK1 dimerization that is required for immune signaling (Liu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Liu et al., 2012.

claim: Pathogens secrete effectors to deregulate host immunity in an evolutionary arms race.
source: The evolution of interactions between microbial pathogens and their hosts involves a continuous arms race, in which pathogens secrete effectors to deregulate host immunity (de Jonge et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Cladosporium fulvum abundantly secretes the LysM-containing effector protein Ecp6 during colonization of tomato.
source: The leaf mold fungus Cladosporium fulvum abundantly secretes the LysM-containing effector protein Ecp6 (for extracellular protein 6; Bolton et al., 2008) during colonization of its host tomato.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Bolton et al., 2008.

claim: Ecp6 acts as a scavenger of chitin fragments and prevents recognition of the fungus by host immune receptors.
source: Ecp6 acts as a scavenger of chitin fragments and thus prevents recognition of the fungus by host immune receptors (de Jonge et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to de Jonge et al., 2010.

claim: Ecp6 homologs occur throughout the fungal kingdom.
source: Intriguingly, Ecp6 homologs occur throughout the fungal kingdom, suggesting a fundamental role of chitin scavenging in fungal pathogenicity (Bolton et al., 2008; de Jonge and Thomma, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The occurrence of Ecp6 homologs throughout the fungal kingdom suggests a fundamental role of chitin scavenging in fungal pathogenicity.
source: Intriguingly, Ecp6 homologs occur throughout the fungal kingdom, suggesting a fundamental role of chitin scavenging in fungal pathogenicity (Bolton et al., 2008; de Jonge and Thomma, 2009).
evidence: This is an inference based on the widespread occurrence of Ecp6 homologs, supported by citations.

claim: LysM effectors from Mycosphaerella graminicola and Magnaporthe oryzae suppress chitin-triggered immunity.
source: Indeed, LysM effectors from the fungal wheat pathogen Mycosphaerella graminicola and the rice pathogen Magnaporthe oryzae suppress chitin-triggered immunity (Marshall et al., 2011; Mentlak et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Marshall et al., 2011 and Mentlak et al., 2012.

claim: LysM-containing proteins are broadly distributed in bacteria, plants, fungi, and animals.
source: LysM-containing proteins are broadly distributed in bacteria, plants, fungi, and animals (Buist et al., 2008; Kombrink et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Only few tertiary LysM structures have been reported in addition to that of AtCERK1.
source: Nevertheless, only few tertiary LysM structures have been reported in addition to that of AtCERK1 (Bateman and Bycroft, 2000; Bielnicki et al., 2006; Koharudin et al., 2011; Liu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous structural studies.

claim: The canonical three-dimensional LysM domain structure consists of a βααβ-fold.
source: The canonical three-dimensional LysM domain structure consists of a βααβ-fold, in which two α-helices are packed against one side of a two-stranded antiparallel β-sheet.
evidence: This is established structural knowledge.

claim: LysM domains physically interact with chitin oligomers in a 1:1 stoichiometry with an affinity binding constant of up to 21 µM based on NMR spectroscopy.
source: Based on NMR spectroscopy, the loop between the first β-sheet and the first α-helix and the loop between the second α-helix and the second β-sheet were shown to physically interact with chitin oligomers in a 1:1 stoichiometry with an affinity binding constant of up to 21 µM (Ohnuma et al., 2008; Koharudin et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous NMR studies.

claim: The AtCERK1 ectodomain binds chitin oligomers with an affinity up to 45 µM for (GlcNAc)8 as determined by isothermal titration calorimetry.
source: The AtCERK1 ectodomain binds chitin oligomers with a similar affinity, up to 45 µM for (GlcNAc)8, as determined by isothermal titration calorimetry (Liu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Liu et al., 2012.

claim: Ecp6 was heterologously produced in the yeast Pichia pastoris and purified.
source: To this end, Ecp6 was heterologously produced in the yeast Pichia pastoris and purified.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental method used.

claim: The Ecp6 crystal structure was determined to a resolution of 1.6 Å.
source: The structure was determined by single-wavelength anomalous dispersion (SAD) and refined to a resolution of 1.6 Å with an Rwork and Rfree of 20.3% and 22.5%, respectively (Figure 1 and Table 1).
evidence: This is a description of the crystallographic data.

claim: The Ecp6 structure model comprises amino acid residues 7 to 195 of the mature protein sequence.
source: The structure model comprises nearly the complete mature protein sequence, from amino acid residues 7 to 195.
evidence: This is a description of the structural model.

claim: Residues 1–6 and 196–199 of Ecp6 were not defined in the electron density map, suggesting they occur as flexible tails.
source: Residues 1–6 and 196–199 of the structure were not defined in the electron density map, suggesting that they occur as flexible tails on both ends of the protein.
evidence: This is an inference from the crystallographic data.

claim: Ecp6 has a tightly packed structure stabilized by four disulfide bridges.
source: Ecp6 has a tightly packed structure that is stabilized by four disulfide bridges, and two spatially close glycosylation sites (Asn104 and Asn193) were identified.
evidence: This is a description of structural features observed in the crystal structure.

claim: Two spatially close glycosylation sites (Asn104 and Asn193) were identified in Ecp6.
source: Ecp6 has a tightly packed structure that is stabilized by four disulfide bridges, and two spatially close glycosylation sites (Asn104 and Asn193) were identified.
evidence: This is a description of structural features observed in the crystal structure.

claim: LysM1 is separated by a long and flexible linker from a compact and rigid body formed by LysM2 and LysM3.
source: The three LysMs of Ecp6 (LysM1–LysM3) share the typical βααβ-fold, with LysM1 being separated by a long and flexible linker from a compact and rigid body formed by LysM2 and LysM3 (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a description of structural features observed in the crystal structure.

claim: The crystal packing revealed the existence of an Ecp6 homodimer.
source: Furthermore, the crystal packing revealed the existence of an Ecp6 homodimer that was also observed in gel filtration chromatography during protein purification, with a flat buried surface of 943 Å2 at LysM2 and LysM3 as calculated using PISA (Protein Interfaces, Surfaces and Assemblies; http://www.ebi.ac.uk/pdbe/prot_int/pistart.html; Figure 1A; Krissinel and Henrick, 2007).
evidence: This is a description of structural features observed in the crystal structure and confirmed by gel filtration.

claim: The Ecp6 homodimer was also observed in gel filtration chromatography during protein purification.
source: Furthermore, the crystal packing revealed the existence of an Ecp6 homodimer that was also observed in gel filtration chromatography during protein purification, with a flat buried surface of 943 Å2 at LysM2 and LysM3 as calculated using PISA (Protein Interfaces, Surfaces and Assemblies; http://www.ebi.ac.uk/pdbe/prot_int/pistart.html; Figure 1A; Krissinel and Henrick, 2007).
evidence: This is a description of experimental observations.

claim: The Ecp6 homodimer has a flat buried surface of 943 Å2 at LysM2 and LysM3.
source: Furthermore, the crystal packing revealed the existence of an Ecp6 homodimer that was also observed in gel filtration chromatography during protein purification, with a flat buried surface of 943 Å2 at LysM2 and LysM3 as calculated using PISA (Protein Interfaces, Surfaces and Assemblies; http://www.ebi.ac.uk/pdbe/prot_int/pistart.html; Figure 1A; Krissinel and Henrick, 2007).
evidence: This is a calculated value from the structural data.

claim: A chitin tetramer (GlcNAc)4 was bound in a large interdomain groove between LysM1 and LysM3 in the Ecp6 crystal structure.
source: Unexpectedly, the calculated 2Fo−Fc map showed a well-defined electron density for a bound chitin tetramer (GlcNAc)4 in a large interdomain groove between LysM1 and LysM3 (∼16 Å long and ∼11 Å across its widest points; Figure 1B), although the protein crystallized in the absence of exogenously added chitin.
evidence: This is a description of structural features observed in the crystal structure.

claim: The interdomain groove between LysM1 and LysM3 is approximately 16 Å long and 11 Å across its widest points.
source: Unexpectedly, the calculated 2Fo−Fc map showed a well-defined electron density for a bound chitin tetramer (GlcNAc)4 in a large interdomain groove between LysM1 and LysM3 (∼16 Å long and ∼11 Å across its widest points; Figure 1B), although the protein crystallized in the absence of exogenously added chitin.
evidence: This is a measurement from the structural data.

claim: The chitin oligomer co-purified with Ecp6 was likely derived from the cell wall of the P. pastoris expression system.
source: The chitin oligomer was likely co-purified with Ecp6 and derived from the cell wall of the P. pastoris expression system.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of chitin in the structure despite no exogenous addition.

claim: The observation that chitin remained adhered to Ecp6 during purification suggests it is bound with high affinity.
source: The observation that the chitin oligomer remained adhered to Ecp6 during the protein purification procedure suggests that it is bound to the groove with high affinity.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental observation.

claim: The chitin-binding groove is shaped by amino acids 20GDTLT24 and 46PNLIEL51 of LysM1 and 150GDLFV154 and 176PSKL179 of LysM3.
source: Specifically, the groove is shaped by the amino acids 20GDTLT24 and 46PNLIEL51 of LysM1 and 150GDLFV154 and 176PSKL179 of LysM3.
evidence: This is a description of structural features observed in the crystal structure.

claim: The chitin binding involves 12 hydrogen bonds between Ecp6 and the chitin tetramer.
source: Evidently, LysM1 and LysM3 of Ecp6 cooperate to bring two chitin-binding regions together, composing a novel type of binding groove in which one chitin tetramer is nearly completely buried and engaged in many noncovalent interactions, including 12 hydrogen bonds (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a description of structural features observed in the crystal structure and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Chitin binding is further strengthened by noncovalent interactions among proximate residues on the complementary surfaces of LysM1 (N45 and 47NLIE50) and LysM3 (150GDLFVD155).
source: The chitin binding is further strengthened by noncovalent interactions among proximate residues on the complementary surfaces of LysM1 (N45 and 47NLIE50) and LysM3 (150GDLFVD155) (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a description of structural features observed in the crystal structure.

claim: The solute-exposed ends of the chitin tetramer in the structure suggest that longer oligomers can also be bound to the groove.
source: Furthermore, the solute-exposed ends of the chitin tetramer in the structure suggest that longer oligomers can also be bound to the groove, in which case four GlcNAc units of a chitin oligomer make direct contact with the protein while the remaining parts of the molecule protrude into the solvent (Figure 1).
evidence: This is an inference from the structural data.

claim: Mutants T22R and N47K in LysM1 resulted in an autoactive protein that triggered a response of tomato cells in the absence of chitin.
source: Unfortunately, the two mutants that were generated in LysM1 (T22R and N47K) resulted in an autoactive protein that triggered a response of the tomato cells, leading to medium alkalinization already in the absence of chitin (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a description of experimental results shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The induction of medium pH shift by the mutants in LysM1 was likely due to improper protein folding.
source: Most probably the induction of medium pH shift by the mutants in LysM1 was due to improper protein folding, as is suggested by CD spectra when compared with wild-type Ecp6 protein (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is an inference based on CD spectroscopy data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The CD spectra of the two mutants in LysM3 (L152R and S177K) were very similar to that of wild-type Ecp6 protein.
source: In contrast, the CD spectra of the two mutants in LysM3 (L152R and S177K) were very similar to that of wild-type Ecp6 protein, indicating that they adopt the same secondary structure (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a description of CD spectroscopy data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Mutants L152R and S177K in LysM3 still prevented chitohexaose-induced medium alkalinization.
source: Interestingly, both mutants still prevented chitohexaose [(GlcNAc)6]-induced medium alkalinization.
evidence: This is a description of experimental results.

claim: LysM2 contributes to the suppression of chitin-triggered immunity by P. pastoris-produced Ecp6 in the cell suspension assay.
source: These results suggest that also LysM2 contributes to the suppression of chitin-triggered immunity by P. pastoris-produced Ecp6 in the cell suspension assay (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental results shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Mutants T95R and D121K in LysM2 no longer suppressed the chitin oligosaccharide-induced pH shift.
source: Interestingly, mutants T95R and D121K no longer suppressed the chitin oligosaccharide-induced pH shift, revealing that LysM2 contains a functional chitin-binding site that contributes to the suppression of chitin-triggered immunity in the cell suspension assay (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a description of experimental results shown in Figure 5A.

claim: ITC experiments confirmed that P. pastoris-produced mutants T95R and D121K were impaired in the binding of exogenously added chitohexaose.
source: Indeed, ITC experiments confirmed that the P. pastoris-produced mutants T95R and D121K were impaired in the binding of exogenously added chitohexaose (Figure 5C and 5D).
evidence: This is a description of ITC experimental results shown in Figures 5C and 5D.

claim: P. pastoris-produced Ecp6 binds chitin with 1:1 stoichiometry and a dissociation constant (kd) of 4.5 µM.
source: Therefore, we integrated the heat measurements using a single binding site model, confirming that P. pastoris-produced Ecp6 binds chitin with 1:1 stoichiometry and a dissociation constant (kd) of 4.5 µM (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a description of ITC experimental results shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The T22R mutant in LysM1 binds chitin with a kd of 4.69 µM and n = 0.75.
source: The T22R mutant in LysM1 binds chitin with similar thermodynamic values as Ecp6 produced in P. pastoris (kd = 4.69 µM; n = 0.75; Figure 3D).
evidence: This is a description of ITC experimental results shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Binding by the N47K mutant could be fitted to a 'two binding site' model, with the second binding displaying a kd of 5.2 µM and n = 0.984.
source: Binding by the N47K mutant could be fitted to a 'two binding site' model, revealing that the second binding displayed similar biochemical characteristics (kd = 5.2 µM; n = 0.984) as Ecp6 produced in P. pastoris (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is a description of ITC experimental results shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Chitin-free Ecp6 was obtained from HEK293 mammalian cells.
source: As an alternative strategy, the production of Ecp6 in mammalian (HEK293) cells was pursued. A relatively small amount (4 mg) of chitin-free Ecp6 was obtained from these cells.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental method and result.

claim: Ecp6 protein produced in mammalian cells was able to suppress chitin-triggered immunity in the tomato cell suspension assay.
source: We confirmed that the Ecp6 protein produced in mammalian cells was able to suppress chitin-triggered immunity in the tomato cell suspension assay (Figure 6) and subsequently performed substrate affinity measurements (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a description of experimental results shown in Figure 6.

claim: ITC revealed biphasic binding of the chitin hexamer (GlcNAc)6 to chitin-free Ecp6.
source: Interestingly, ITC revealed biphasic binding of the chitin hexamer (GlcNAc)6 to chitin-free Ecp6.
evidence: This is a description of ITC experimental results.

claim: Chitin-free Ecp6 binds one chitin molecule with ultra-high affinity (kd = 280 pM; n = 0.99) in the first binding phase.
source: A first binding phase in which one chitin molecule was bound with ultra-high affinity (kd = 280 pM; n = 0.99) occurred, followed by binding of an additional molecule with lower affinity (kd = 1.70 µM; n = 1.03) (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is a description of ITC experimental results shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Chitin-free Ecp6 binds an additional chitin molecule with lower affinity (kd = 1.70 µM; n = 1.03) in the second binding phase.
source: A first binding phase in which one chitin molecule was bound with ultra-high affinity (kd = 280 pM; n = 0.99) occurred, followed by binding of an additional molecule with lower affinity (kd = 1.70 µM; n = 1.03) (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is a description of ITC experimental results shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Both binding events of chitin-free Ecp6 displayed 1:1 stoichiometry.
source: Both binding events displayed 1:1 stoichiometry, demonstrating that the three LysM domains of a single Ecp6 monomer are collectively involved in two binding events (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is a description of ITC experimental results shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The three LysM domains of a single Ecp6 monomer are collectively involved in two binding events.
source: Both binding events displayed 1:1 stoichiometry, demonstrating that the three LysM domains of a single Ecp6 monomer are collectively involved in two binding events (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is an inference from the ITC experimental results shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The µM affinity binding event should be attributed to LysM2.
source: As P. pastoris-produced Ecp6, in which the LysM1–LysM3 groove is blocked by a P. pastoris chitin fragment, displayed similar characteristics as the second binding event of mammalian cell-produced Ecp6 (Figure 7A,B), we conclude that the µM affinity should be attributed to LysM2.
evidence: This is an inference from comparing ITC results shown in Figures 7A and 7B.

claim: The HEK293-produced LysM2 mutant T95R binds a single chitin molecule with high affinity (kd = 4.95 nM).
source: To confirm this hypothesis, we also produced the LysM2 mutant T95R, which only has the LysM1–LysM3 site available for chitin binding, in mammalian cells. As this mutant binds a single chitin molecule with high affinity (kd = 4.95 nM) (Figure 7C), we concluded that the ultra-high chitin-binding affinity displayed by wild-type Ecp6 corresponds to the LysM1–LysM3 binding groove.
evidence: This is a description of ITC experimental results shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The ultra-high chitin-binding affinity displayed by wild-type Ecp6 corresponds to the LysM1–LysM3 binding groove.
source: As this mutant binds a single chitin molecule with high affinity (kd = 4.95 nM) (Figure 7C), we concluded that the ultra-high chitin-binding affinity displayed by wild-type Ecp6 corresponds to the LysM1–LysM3 binding groove.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the ITC experimental results shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The HEK293-produced LysM2 mutant T95R was able to prevent chitin-triggered medium alkalinization.
source: We subsequently analyzed the role of the LysM1–LysM3 groove in suppression of chitin-triggered immunity in the tomato cell suspension assay with the HEK293-produced LysM2 mutant T95R. As expected, this mutant protein was able to prevent chitin-triggered medium alkalinization (Figure 6).
evidence: This is a description of experimental results shown in Figure 6.

claim: The composite LysM1–LysM3 binding site provides a single binding event with ultra-high (pM) affinity for chitin binding, the highest chitin-binding affinity described in nature.
source: Consequently, the composite LysM1–LysM3 binding site provides a single binding event with ultra-high (pM) affinity for chitin binding, the highest chitin-binding affinity described in nature, which is extremely competent to sequester chitin oligosaccharides.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Through the LysM1-LysM3 binding site, C. fulvum prevents chitin oligosaccharides from activating host immune receptors during infection of tomato.
source: Through this effector activity, C. fulvum prevents chitin oligosaccharides from activating host immune receptors during infection of tomato.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: The flexible loop between LysM1 and the rigid LysM2–LysM3 body enables the sandwiching of four GlcNAc units of a chitin oligomer in the interface of the LysM1–LysM3 dimer.
source: The flexible loop between LysM1 and the rigid LysM2–LysM3 body enables the sandwiching of four GlcNAc units of a chitin oligomer in the interface of the LysM1–LysM3 dimer by 12 hydrogen bonds and many other noncovalent interactions, resulting in ultra-high (pM) affinity.
evidence: This is a description of the structural mechanism based on the crystal structure.

claim: The intrachain LysM dimerization in Ecp6 is anticipated to be substrate induced rather than pre-formed.
source: Based on the structure of the binding groove, it is anticipated that the intrachain LysM dimerization is substrate induced rather than pre-formed, as the chitin oligomer is completely buried in between the two LysM domains that are in very close proximity to make contact with the chitin oligomer.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural data.

claim: A pre-formed binding site would require a chitin oligomer to slide along the two LysM domain binding sites, which is practically impossible.
source: A pre-formed binding site would require a chitin oligomer to slide along the two LysM domain binding sites, which is practically impossible.
evidence: This is a logical argument based on the structural data.

claim: The binding groove significantly opens in absence of the ligand and closes upon ligand binding, leading to substrate-induced intrachain LysM domain dimerization.
source: More realistically, and considering the long and flexible linker that separates LysM1 from the LysM2–LysM3 body, the binding groove significantly opens in absence of the ligand and closes upon ligand binding, leading to substrate-induced intrachain LysM domain dimerization.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural data and the flexible linker.

claim: Longer chitin oligomers may protrude from the Ecp6 protein into the solvent on both ends.
source: Longer chitin oligomers may protrude from the Ecp6 protein into the solvent on both ends, which is particularly relevant since these are considered to be the most biologically active in eliciting chitin-triggered immune responses (Felix et al., 1993; Liu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural data, supported by citations.

claim: Previously determined affinity constants were similar for chitin tetra-, penta-, hexa- and octamers binding to Ecp6.
source: Indeed, previously determined affinity constants were similar for chitin tetra-, penta-, hexa- and octamers (de Jonge et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to de Jonge et al., 2010.

claim: As soon as Ecp6 is secreted from the plasma membrane of C. fulvum, it will sequester a chitin oligosaccharide that remains firmly attached to the protein.

evidence: This is a calculation based on the measured dissociation constant and experimental concentrations.

claim: The C. fulvum LysM effector Ecp6 is able to suppress chitin-triggered immunity through two mechanisms: efficient chitin oligosaccharide sequestration through a ligand-induced composite LysM1–LysM3 binding groove, and a mechanism exerted by LysM2 that does not involve chitin oligosaccharide sequestration but may involve perturbation of host immune receptor complexes.
source: In conclusion, it appears that the C. fulvum LysM effector Ecp6 is able to suppress chitin-triggered immunity through two mechanisms; efficient chitin oligosaccharide sequestration through a ligand-induced composite LysM1–LysM3 binding groove, and secondly a mechanism exerted by LysM2 that does not involve chitin oligosaccharide sequestration but may involve perturbation of host immune receptor complexes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Convergent evolution towards recognition of the same ligand by molecules of taxonomically diverse organisms frequently occurs.
source: Convergent evolution towards recognition of the same ligand by molecules of taxonomically diverse organisms frequently occurs, as exemplified by the perception of bacterial flagellin by the mammalian and plant immune receptors TLR5 and FLS2, although these receptors recognize different PAMP motifs within the same ligand (Felix et al., 1999; Smith et al., 2003; Chinchilla et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Mammalian and plant immune receptors TLR5 and FLS2 perceive bacterial flagellin but recognize different PAMP motifs within the same ligand.

Consequently, the suppression of chitin-triggered immunity by LysM2 is unlikely to work via chitin oligosaccharide sequestration.
